name: Sociedade Vegetariana Brasileira: institutional meal replacement (charityevals)
summary: Sociedade Vegetariana Brasileira (SVB) helps Brazilian public schools, popular restaurants, social-assistance centres and companies serve plant-based meals on one or more days a week (the Segunda Sem Carne program), through menu design, recipes and cook training; it says partners have served over 530 million such meals since 2009. We model this institutional program only: about 35 million meals a year (inferred from SVB's cumulative counts), each with roughly 43 g of meat, for an estimated 20% of SVB's 2023 program spending. Our best guess is about 19 SADs averted per dollar, roughly 5× GiveDirectly. The biggest uncertainties are what a replaced meal is worth in animal suffering, how much of the program's continuing output still depends on SVB, and SVB's self-reported, unverified meal counts. The result is mostly uncertainty: with every input at its low or high end it runs from near zero to over 1,000× GiveDirectly, largely because of the shared exchange rates between animal suffering and human welfare.

rows.label: Share of program costs spent on institutional meal programs (Segunda Sem Carne)
rows.explainer:
SVB's statements don't split costs by program, so this is our estimate. Its team page (current, retrieved 2026, so only a proxy for 2023) lists 42 names, including board members who are unpaid. Six have titles specific to institutional food programs: the manager and two analysts of food programs and policy, the institutional-partnerships analyst, the government-relations specialist and the consultant cook who trains kitchen staff; the 7-person nutrition department contributes part of its time. Against them: 5 in vegan certification (Selo Vegano, which earns service revenue), 3 in events, about 5 in communication, design and marketing, plus finance, membership and volunteering. Headcount puts the institutional program at about 20% of program staff, our best guess.

Low (12%): only the six dedicated roles, at average pay. High (40%): most nutrition, culinary, communication and government-relations work counted as institutional, or the program's partner events and materials cost more than its share of staff. A higher share means more cost per meal, so a lower result.

Plant-based meals served through SVB's institutional partners per year (around 2023)

source.title: SVB, Comemoração dos 15 anos da Segunda Sem Carne no Brasil (18 Oct 2024); segundasemcarne.com.br, A Campanha
source.quote: já foram servidas mais de 530 milhões de refeições com proteína vegetal

rows.explainer:
SVB publishes cumulative, not annual, meal counts for its institutional program (Segunda Sem Carne: one or more plant-based days in public schools, the Bom Prato popular restaurants, social-assistance centres, hospitals and companies). Our annual figure is the difference between its cumulative totals: 327 million at the 10-year mark (July 2019, segundasemcarne.com.br), 'more than 500 million' in a 2023 entry on the same page, and more than 530 million by October 2024. That is about 39 million a year from mid-2019 to late 2024, including the 2020–21 school closures, and roughly 30 million in the last year or so. SVB's last annual figures were 47 million (2017, TNH1) and 67 million (2018, svb.org.br); SVB material also cites over 80 million for 2019, which we saw only in a search summary and don't rely on. The latest increment (over 500 million on 1 October 2023 to over 530 million in October 2024) covers a window about nine months later than the 2023 cost year; we treat the program as roughly steady over that period. SVB doesn't say how it counts meals; the campaign's timeline shows the count includes company canteens and hospitals as well as public schools and restaurants.

Best guess 35 million meals in 2023. Low (20 million): the cumulative counts are rounded ('more than') and the recent increment could be smaller. High (55 million): a partial recovery toward the pre-pandemic level. These are SVB's own counts, not independently verified; how far they translate into meals actually eaten is in the delivery adjustment.

rows.label: Meat per replaced meal (grams)

source.title: SVB, Segunda Sem Carne do Brasil é a maior do mundo; TNH1 (24 Apr 2018)
source.quote: Juntos, os programas pouparam, neste ano de 2017, nada menos do que duas mil toneladas de carne.

rows.explainer: Our estimate of the meat in one replaced meal, from SVB's own 2017 figures: 2,000 tonnes of meat not served (svb.org.br, covering São Paulo's city and state schools, state social programs, Bom Prato and 'others') divided by 47 million meals that year ('Só em 2017 foram 47 milhões de refeições Segunda sem Carne na rede pública', SVB's campaign manager to TNH1, 24 Apr 2018) is about 43 g, a child's school-lunch portion. The two figures come from different sources and may not cover the same programs. A sub-figure for São Paulo's municipal schools (about 1 million pupils, 436 tonnes a year) gives 22–43 g depending on whether each pupil gets 10 or 20 meatless meals a year, which SVB doesn't state. Range 25 g (smaller school portions, or the tonnage covers fewer meals than we assume) to 60 g (more adult meals from Bom Prato and company canteens).

rows.label: Meat in the typical meal behind the shared SADs-per-meal figure (grams)
rows.explainer: The shared SADs-per-meal figure's best value comes from Sinergia Animal's institutional program: its data sheet lists 25 canteens in Argentina, Colombia and Indonesia, mostly school, university and community kitchens serving children and adults (e.g. 'Coordinación de Comedores - Gualeguaychú (21 schools)'), so the reference meal is a canteen meal of the same kind as SVB's, not an adult restaurant portion. The sheet doesn't state grams of meat or how its per-meal values were derived, and it gives every institution in a country the same value (0.60 for all Argentine rows, from a university canteen to a hospital), which suggests an average national meal rather than a measured canteen portion. So this is our judgment: best 60 g, between a mixed child/adult canteen meal (about 50 g) and an average adult meal. Low 35 g (the reference is a children's school meal like SVB's); high 100 g (the reference is an average adult meal with a full meat portion). Only the ratio to SVB's portions matters; at the best values SVB's meals carry about 72% of the reference meal's meat.

rows.label: SADs per meal for Brazil's meat mix, relative to the shared figure

source.title: Sinergia Animal, Nourishing Tomorrow impact data ('NT impact' tab), linked from ACE's Sinergia Animal CEA (2025)
source.page: NT impact tab, SADs-per-meal column: Argentina rows 0.60, Colombia rows 0.88

rows.explainer: How much suffering a replaced meal involves depends on the species in it: chicken and fish mean many more animals per gram than beef. The shared best value (0.90 SADs per meal) is a meal-weighted mean of the per-country values on the sheet behind it: 0.60 for Argentina (beef-heavy), 0.88 for Colombia and 4.28 for Indonesia, which pulls the mean up. Where Brazil sits between them is our judgment, not a sourced figure: Brazil's school menus mix beef and chicken, between Argentina and Colombia, so we put Brazil at about 0.72, 80% of the shared value. Low (65%): an Argentina-like, beef-heavy mix. High (100%): the shared value as is, if chicken and eggs dominate the replaced protein.

rows.label: SVB's replaced meal relative to a typical meal (by meat content)
rows.explainer: SVB's replaced meals, mostly children's school lunches, contain somewhat less meat than the mixed canteen meal behind the shared figure, so each averts proportionally less suffering.

rows.label: SADs averted per meal replaced
rows.explainer: The shared figure for one animal-product meal, scaled by how much meat SVB's meals contained (SVB reports both meals and tonnes of meat saved) and by Brazil's meat mix (about 0.6 SADs per meal at the best values). The shared figure's range (0.084–1.72) already spans meal composition (chicken- and fish-heavy meals involve far more animals than beef), and its low end is another evaluator's figure for these same institutional meals; with our portion scaling on top, the joint low end is pessimistic. We keep the shared range so this model stays comparable with other diet-change models.

rows.label: Fall in production per meal not eaten
rows.explainer: Fewer meals bought lowers production by less than one for one, because prices fall and others buy more. Public-school purchasing in Brazil is large, but the meat it doesn't buy still enters a national market, so the usual elasticity applies. The shared best value (0.76) is chicken's; for beef, which is common on Brazilian school menus, Norwood and Lusk give 0.68, about 10% lower and inside the shared range.

rows.label: Years of meals one year of SVB's work accounts for
rows.explainer: One year, by construction. The meals above are the yearly flow from all of SVB's partnerships, old and new, and we credit each year of spending with one year of that flow. Crediting more (for instance for the future meals of partnerships started this year) would count those meals twice, because next year's spending is credited with next year's flow, which includes them. How much of the flow depends on SVB's current work, rather than on menus that would continue anyway, is the counterfactual adjustment.

rows.label: Discounted years of impact
rows.explainer: With one year of impact counted from the start of the year, no discounting applies.

rows.label: Evidence adjustment (does a meal served reduce consumption?)
rows.explainer:
Given that a plant-based meal was served and eaten, does the person eat fewer animal products overall that day? No study measures this for SVB's program, and we found none on compensation at home after school meatless days. Two effects reduce it: people eating more meat at other meals (compensation), and 'plant-protein' meals that use eggs or cheese, which still involve animals. Pupils who skip the meal or take less are in the delivery adjustment, not here.

Best 0.75: about a quarter of the effect lost to compensation and substitution. Low (0.5): substantial compensation, as when families serve meat at dinner to make up for it. High (0.95): little compensation; for many low-income pupils the school meal is the main meal of the day, and Bom Prato diners are low-income adults.

rows.label: Share of the meals that wouldn't be plant-based without SVB
rows.explainer: Most of the year's meals come from partnerships SVB set up years ago (São Paulo's city schools since 2011, the state schools and Bom Prato restaurants since the mid-2010s). Some of those menus would now continue without SVB's ongoing support: Helsinki's vegetarian school day, for instance, has kept running for over a decade, and other groups now run their own Brazilian school-meal programs (Humane World for Animals reports one in Fortaleza), so some municipalities might have adopted similar menus without SVB. Others would not: none rests on a legal mandate we could confirm (Santos's council passed a Segunda Sem Carne bill at first reading in 2016; we couldn't confirm it became law). São Paulo state's 'Segunda Sem Carne' bill passed the legislature but was vetoed by the governor (Agrolink, 22 Jan 2018: 'O governador de São Paulo, Geraldo Alckmin (PSDB), vetou nesta sexta-feira o projeto de lei'), and a federal bill (PL 4624/12) was rejected in committee (Câmara dos Deputados, 2015). The menus are administrative choices of each municipal or state administration, open to reversal under farm-lobby pressure or a change of government, and SVB keeps working with partners after launch (recipe refreshes, cook training, e.g. the 2023 Jacareí recipe update on the campaign page). We found no case data on partners that kept or dropped the meatless day after SVB's support ended, so this remains a judgment. Best 50%. Low (25%): most partners would keep their meatless day anyway. High (80%): partners rely on SVB's training, recipes and follow-up to keep going. The credit for meals that other groups also helped set up is the attribution share, not this.

rows.label: SVB's share of credit, when shared with others
rows.explainer: Municipal nutritionists and politicians decide on and serve the meals, and other groups work on some of the same partnerships: Humane Society International worked with SVB and Mercy For Animals in Passo Fundo and on a 15-school Rio de Janeiro pilot (Humane World for Animals blog, 26 Jan 2026: 'Together with Mercy For Animals and Brazilian Vegetarian Society, we secured a new commitment'). Most of SVB's cumulative count, though, comes from partnerships it led itself. Best 70%. Low (40%): equal sharing with partner NGOs and the municipalities. High (90%): SVB alone for the São Paulo programs that dominate the count.

rows.label: Share of credit used
rows.explainer: The charity's share of the resources behind the outcome; it applies whichever way credit is shared.

rows.label: Delivery adjustment (meals actually served and eaten as reported)
rows.explainer: SVB's meal counts are its own: likely meals planned on menus (pupils enrolled × meatless days) rather than meals served and eaten, and they are not independently verified. Schools miss days and menus slip back. Fewer pupils may take the meal on the vegetarian day, and those who do may take less and waste more: Helsinki's mandatory weekly vegetarian school day showed all three at first, with only smaller helpings persisting in the medium term (Lombardini and Lankoski, 2013). This adjustment is the only place those effects are counted. Best 70% of the reported meals actually served and eaten as a plant-based replacement. Low (40%): counts based on enrolment and plans, with marked non-take-up. High (90%): counts close to meals eaten.

rows.label: All adjustments combined
rows.explainer: The product of the adjustments above.

source.quote: Custos com Pessoal (276.015,52) Custos com Assessorias e Consultorias (1.683.375,40)

rows.explainer: Employees cost R$276,016 in 2023 (9% of total expenses), but most of SVB's team works as contracted consultants (R$1,683,375, 56%), as is common in Brazil. We count most consulting fees as staff pay: best 45% of total costs. Low (25%): half of the consulting fees are outside services. High (65%): all of it plus employees. Board and directors are unpaid (note 14).

rows.label: Pay gap versus comparable for-profit jobs
rows.explainer: How much less SVB's staff earn than in comparable roles. The repo's reference points are about 15% for large delivery charities and 35% for advocacy groups. SVB is a small advocacy and technical-assistance group with unpaid directors (which would argue for the advocacy figure), but most of its team bills as contracted consultants, who in Brazil often charge near market rates. We take 20%. Low (5%): consultants paid at market rates. High (35%): the advocacy-group reference.
